terms.definition: Google's library for neural networks; code calls it tf.
the part of TensorFlow used to build and train neural networks.
a model built from many small parts (neurons) arranged in layers; each part does a little arithmetic and passes its result on.
machine learning with neural networks of many layers.
a group of neurons working side by side; a network is several layers, each feeding the next.
a number the network learns; each input is multiplied by its weight.
70,000 small (28 × 28 pixel) photos of handwritten digits 0–9, a standard beginner's dataset.
TensorFlow's standard export: a folder holding the computation graph, the weights and the signatures, loadable without your Python code.
the fixed list of operations, in order, that turn an input into an output.
the declared name, type and shape of a saved model's inputs and outputs; serving_default is the one Keras creates.
a computation graph plus its signatures, labelled with a tag such as serve.
write the trained model to disk in a standard format so another program can use it.
a subfolder named with a zero-padded number (0001, 0002) that holds one version of the exported model.
the steps that turn raw input into what the model expects, e.g. scaling pixels from 0–255 to 0–1.
a command-line tool that lists what a SavedModel contains.
TensorFlow's name for an array of numbers, of any number of dimensions.
a number between 0 and 1 saying how likely something is; the model gives one per digit, adding up to 1.
a TensorFlow operation that runs ordinary Python code; it cannot be saved in a graph.
TensorFlow Serving: a ready-made server program that loads SavedModels from a folder and answers prediction requests over the network.
a program (or machine) that waits for requests and answers them.
the program that sends a request to a server and uses the answer.
using a trained model to make predictions (as opposed to training it).
a numbered door on a computer that a server listens on; TF Serving uses 8500 (gRPC) and 8501 (REST).
application programming interface: the fixed set of requests a program accepts from other programs.
calling a server with ordinary web (HTTP) requests carrying JSON text.
the protocol web browsers and servers use to send requests and answers.
an HTTP request that sends data to the server, here the images to predict.
a text format for data: lists in [ ], named fields in { }.
a way to call a server that sends compact binary messages instead of JSON text.
a message whose fields are declared in advance in a schema and sent as compact binary.
a local object whose method calls are turned into network calls to the server.
the caller waits, doing nothing else, until the answer (or a timeout) arrives.
how long a call may wait before it gives up with an error.
turning an in-memory value into bytes that can be sent or stored; deserialization is the reverse.
.tolist() turns a NumPy array into ordinary Python lists, which JSON can write.
encryption for network connections; an insecure channel has none.
a tool that runs a program in a container, isolated from the rest of the computer.
a packaged program plus everything it needs, run isolated from the host computer.
the packaged file a container is started from, named by an address such as gcr.io/…
a named setting given to a program by the operating system, outside its code.
a signing key that proves downloaded packages come from who they claim to.
Google Colab: free notebooks that run on Google's machines in the browser.
switching to a new version without dropping a request: new requests go to it, the old one finishes its work first.
let a version go idle: it takes no new work and is unloaded after its last request.
running a new model on sample inputs before it serves, so the first real requests are not slow.
going back to the previous version after a bad release.
a component that shares incoming requests out between several identical servers.
one of several identical copies (of a server, or of a model during training).
how long one request takes to be answered.
how many requests (or examples) are handled per second.
Google's rented computing service (GCP): machines, storage and managed services, paid by use.
Google Cloud's managed machine-learning service: it trains, stores and serves models for you.
the container every Google Cloud resource belongs to; its ID is chosen once and never changes.
the paid account a cloud project charges its costs to.
a free Linux command line in the browser, already set up for Google Cloud.
Google's command-line tools for driving Google Cloud.
a named container of files in Google Cloud Storage (GCS), addressed as gs://bucket/…
storage that keeps whole files by name in a flat space, like S3, MinIO or GCS.
the standard way a person grants a program temporary access to their account.
an identity that belongs to a program rather than a person, with only the permissions its role gives.
a named set of permissions, e.g. Vertex AI user.
proving who (or which program) is making a request.
the address clients call for predictions; on Vertex AI, a running service with one or more models behind it.
adding machines automatically when traffic rises and removing them when it falls.
the part of the world where cloud machines run, e.g. us-central1.
the size of a rented cloud machine; n1-standard-4 has 4 virtual CPUs.
extra hardware, usually a GPU, that speeds up the maths.
a job that reads a whole file of inputs, writes all the predictions to files, then stops.
started now, finishing on its own schedule; the caller does not wait for it.
a text file with one JSON value per line.
TensorFlow's binary file format for a list of examples.
a Vertex AI job that runs your own training script on machines it rents for you.
environment variables Vertex AI sets to tell a training script where to save the model, checkpoints and logs.
a copy of the model saved during training, so a crashed job can resume.
TensorFlow's tool for viewing training curves and logs.
an object Keras calls at fixed moments during training, e.g. to save a checkpoint.
TensorFlow's file functions; they work on local files and on gs:// paths alike.
searching automatically for the hyperparameter values that give the best validation score.
a search that picks each next try where the results so far suggest the most gain.
a trial is one training run with one set of hyperparameters; a study is all the trials of one search.
a small Google library a training script uses to report its score to the tuning service.
Python's standard way to read settings given on the command line.
a scale where each step multiplies the value (0.001, 0.01, 0.1 …) instead of adding to it.
a library that runs hyperparameter searches; its chief machine (the oracle) hands out the values to try.
running the model on the device where the data is (a phone, a sensor) rather than on a server.
the version of TensorFlow for phones and small devices; it converts models to a compact .tflite file.
a file format laid out exactly as it is used in memory, so it loads without being parsed.
replacing two operations by one that does both, e.g. folding batch normalization into the layer before it.
a layer that rescales its inputs to a steady range during training.
storing numbers with fewer bits, e.g. 32-bit decimals as 8-bit whole numbers.
float32 = a decimal number stored in 32 bits (4 bytes); int8 = a whole number from −128 to 127 in 8 bits (1 byte).
the numbers flowing between layers while the model runs.
running sample data through the model to measure the range of its activations.
training with simulated rounding, so the final weights still work once quantized.
Google's small chip for running quantized models fast on devices.
the JavaScript version of TensorFlow, which runs models inside a web browser.
the programming language web pages run in the browser.
the browser's standard way to use the graphics card.
a small pretrained image classifier, light enough to download into a browser or phone.
a model someone else already trained, ready to use.
a website that can be installed and opened like a phone or desktop app.
a background browser script that caches files so a web app works offline.
training one model across many devices without collecting their data in one place.
graphics processing unit: a chip with thousands of small cores that does the maths of neural networks far faster than a CPU.
the computer's main processor.
one of the processors inside a CPU (or GPU) that can work at the same time as the others.
the memory on the graphics card itself.
a computer's working memory.
the software that lets the operating system talk to the graphics card.
Nvidia's software for general-purpose computing on its GPUs.
Nvidia's library of fast implementations of neural-network operations such as convolutions.
a command that lists the Nvidia cards, their memory use and the programs using them.
Nvidia's version number for what a card's hardware can do.
a physical device is a real card; a logical device is a slice of one that TensorFlow treats as a whole device.
free memory broken into pieces too small to use.
the error a program gets when it asks for more memory than is free.
environment variables that choose which GPU cards a program may see, and in what order they are numbered.
letting TensorFlow take GPU memory as it needs it instead of all at once (it never gives it back).
which device (CPU or which GPU) a variable or operation runs on; TensorFlow chooses unless you say.
the implementation of one operation for one device and data type; no GPU kernel means it runs on the CPU.
a tensor whose value can be updated, such as a model's weights.
a Python with-block that switches something on for the lines inside it and off after.
if you ask for a device that is not there, TensorFlow silently uses its default choice instead.
a Python function TensorFlow has turned into a graph, so it can plan and parallelize the operations.
for each operation, how many of its inputs are not ready yet; it runs when this reaches 0.
inter-op threads run different operations at the same time; intra-op threads split one operation's work.
one line of work a program runs; several threads can run at once on several cores.
the core arithmetic of neural networks: many multiply-and-add operations over two tables of numbers.
an operation that changes something that stays, such as updating a variable.
splitting one model into pieces that run on different devices.
putting a full copy of the model on every device, each training on a different slice of every batch.
a layer where every input feeds every neuron; Keras calls it a Dense layer.
a network whose layers each look only at small neighbouring patches of the input (used for images).
a network that reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a memory forward (LSTM is a common kind).
each device runs one stage, passing its result on, so all stages work at once on different items.
the small group of training examples used for one training step.
for each weight, how much and in which direction to change it to reduce the error.
one pass of training over the whole training set.
how big a step training takes each time it changes the weights.
the devices exchange their gradients so that every one ends up with the same average.
data parallelism where every GPU holds a full copy of the weights and all copies are updated identically.
a machine (or device) that holds the model's weights centrally while others compute the gradients.
gradients computed with weights that other replicas have already changed.
how much data a connection can carry per second.
a model whose gradients are mostly zeros, so there is little to send between devices.
TensorFlow's way to run the same training code on several devices; you build the model inside strategy.scope().
a group of TensorFlow processes (tasks) on one or more machines, working on one job.
one process in a TensorFlow cluster, with a role (worker, chief …) and a number.
a task that does the model's computations.
the one worker that also writes the logs and checkpoints.
a task that only evaluates the model; rarely used.
an environment variable (read through a resolver) that gives each process the cluster's map and its own role.
the mirrored strategy across several machines, averaging gradients over the network.
an operation every worker must take part in at the same moment, such as AllReduce.
the number that identifies a machine on a network.
the standard way two computers on a network keep a connection open; a TCP port number picks which program on the machine answers.
the size of each dimension of an array, e.g. (3, 28, 28) = 3 images of 28 × 28 pixels; -1 in a shape means "any number".
an activation that keeps a positive sum as it is and turns a negative one into 0.
an output activation that turns the last layer's numbers into probabilities, one per class, adding up to 1.
the one number saying how wrong the model's answers are; training changes the weights to make it smaller.
the method that changes the weights after each batch to lower the loss, e.g. SGD.
the basic optimizer: after each small batch, it moves every weight a small step in the direction that lowers the loss.
the share of examples the model gets right.
the position of the largest value in a list; for our ten probabilities, the predicted digit.
an identity that can be given permissions: a person's account or a service account.
Identity and Access Management: Google Cloud's list of which principal may do what; an IAM binding gives one principal one role.
Cloud Storage's word for one stored file (its bytes plus its name) inside a bucket.
a step in image networks that shrinks an image by keeping one value (the largest, or the average) per small block of pixels.
mebibyte and gibibyte: 1 MiB = 1,024 × 1,024 bytes (about a million), 1 GiB = 1,024 MiB (about a billion bytes). TensorFlow's memory_limit is in MiB.
two ways to cut a network across devices: horizontal = whole layers on different devices; vertical = each layer cut in two, one half per device.
the distribution strategy for TPUs (Tensor Processing Units: Google's own chips for neural-network arithmetic, rented on Google Cloud or Colab).
a model's raw output scores, before softmax turns them into probabilities.
a popular optimizer that gives every weight its own step size, adapted from that weight's recent gradients.
a bucket folder where Vertex AI copies your training script before running it, and where it writes the outputs by default.
said of cheap rented cloud machines that the cloud may take back at any moment; a job on one is "preempted" when that happens.
a training-only step that switches off random neurons at each training step, so the network cannot rely on any single one; it does nothing at prediction time.
